content.headline: Saudi Arabia vows response as Houthi strikes hit airports and oil sites
content.shortHeadline: Saudi vows response to Houthi airport attacks
content.standfirst: A missile attack on Riyadh airport killed 13 people on Saturday, with another fatality reported in a strike the following day. Saudi Arabia says it will respond as the Houthis claim further attacks.

image.caption: Footage from inside Riyadh airport shows the moment a strike hit.

sources.originalTitle: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged
De rammer lufthavne og rørledninger – men hvorfor kan Saudi-Arabien ikke knække houthierne?

segments.body: Saudi Arabia’s energy minister has promised a “serious” response after repeated Houthi attacks on airports and energy facilities. Saudi authorities reported 13 deaths in Saturday’s strike on a Riyadh airport terminal and one more death after a projectile hit another terminal on Sunday. A further missile was intercepted on Monday night.

segments.title: A wider regional risk
segments.body: The attacks come as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces fight to retake territory near the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key route for oil exports. The BBC reports that about 200,000 people have been displaced by the latest escalation. A TV 2 analyst says Saudi Arabia faces difficult choices: air strikes have not defeated the Houthis, while a ground offensive could cost many lives.

perspectives.body: TV 2’s military analyst Peter Viggo Jakobsen argues that without deploying ground forces to seize and hold Houthi territory, it will be very difficult for Saudi Arabia to stop the group’s long-range attacks.

content.headline: Ukraine reports strikes on six energy sites after Trump’s ceasefire claim
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine says Russia hit six energy sites after truce claim
content.standfirst: Kyiv says Russian attacks continued after Donald Trump announced an immediate energy truce. Moscow has not confirmed that it agreed to the arrangement, and reports of a possible US intelligence cutoff remain unconfirmed.

image.caption: Emergency services respond to a Russian drone strike on a residential building in Kharkiv.

sources.originalTitle: Six Ukrainian energy sites hit by Russia since Trump announced ceasefire, Zelensky says
Why Moscow is staying tight-lipped on Trump's energy ceasefire
Ukrainsk politiker: Uden amerikanske efterretninger bliver vores luftforsvar blindt
USA truer med at droppe støtten, hvis Ukraine fortsætter angreb på Rusland

segments.body: President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia struck six Ukrainian energy facilities after Trump declared an energy ceasefire was in force. Ukraine reported power cuts in several regions and introduced electricity rationing in some areas. Russia’s foreign minister said Ukraine did not deserve the “respite” a ceasefire would bring, while Moscow has not confirmed it agreed to one.

segments.title: Pressure over intelligence
segments.body: Several media outlets, citing unnamed officials, reported US threats to stop sharing intelligence and halt weapons procurement if Ukraine continued striking Russian energy sites. Those threats have not been officially confirmed. Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezjko warned that losing US intelligence would leave Ukraine’s air defences “blind”; the extent of any possible cutoff remains unclear.

perspectives.body: Merezjko says US intelligence helps Ukraine detect incoming Russian attacks. The report also notes that European partners contribute intelligence, but cites an expert who says France cannot fully replace the US contribution.

content.headline: Batam residents say data centres are worsening water shortages
content.shortHeadline: Batam residents say data centres threaten water supplies
content.standfirst: Residents on the Indonesian island say their taps have run dry as data-centre construction expands. Authorities blame a prolonged dry spell, and the amount of water used by the centres has not been disclosed.

image.caption: Batam’s reservoirs are under pressure as the island develops as a digital hub.

sources.originalTitle: The island where locals say data centres are taking their water

segments.body: About 300 residents protested at a data-centre compound on Batam after months of unreliable household water. One resident said her village now relies on tanker deliveries of dirty, cloudy water. The island’s water utility says it is working to improve supply, while the agency overseeing trade and industry attributes the shortage to a prolonged dry spell and denies that household water is being diverted to data centres.

segments.title: Demand and accountability
segments.body: Batam relies on rainwater stored in six artificial reservoirs, which are under pressure as the island courts billions of dollars in data-centre investment. Local authorities have told new operators to build desalination plants, but the water and electricity used by the centres remain unclear. A Norwegian University of Science and Technology professor says reliable data on Indonesian data-centre water use is scarce because companies treat it as proprietary.

content.headline: Pupil, 14, arrested after shooting injures two teachers in southern France
content.shortHeadline: Two teachers injured in shooting at French school
content.standfirst: A 14-year-old was arrested after a shooting at a middle school in Aubagne. The principal and a teacher were injured; investigators have opened an attempted-murder inquiry.

image.caption: Police at the school in Aubagne, near Marseille.

sources.originalTitle: Pupil arrested after two teachers shot at French school

segments.body: A pupil entered Lakanal middle school in Aubagne with a shotgun in a guitar case and opened fire, regional officials said. The school principal and a teacher were injured but their wounds are not life-threatening. No children were harmed. A staff member restrained the pupil, and the Marseille prosecutor’s office opened an investigation for attempted murder.

The mayor said students were confined and made safe within seconds, though some were deeply shaken and received psychological support. The school was due to remain closed on Tuesday. Authorities have not established a motive; local media, citing police sources, reported that the shooting was not thought to be connected to protests over school conditions.

content.headline: Trump weighs firing Greece envoy after misconduct allegations
content.shortHeadline: Trump considers firing Greece envoy amid allegations
content.standfirst: Donald Trump says he is considering whether to remove Kimberly Guilfoyle as ambassador to Greece. She denies wrongdoing, and her lawyers dispute the authenticity of messages cited in reports about alleged payments for access.

image.caption: Kimberly Guilfoyle was previously engaged to Donald Trump Jr.

sources.originalTitle: Trump says Kimberly Guilfoyle could be fired as Greece envoy after alleged misconduct
Trump overvejer fyring af ambassadør i Grækenland: Vi er ikke glade
Trumps søns eksforlovede i diplomatisk stormvejr i Athen

segments.body: Trump said he was “looking at” whether to fire Kimberly Guilfoyle after reports of alleged misconduct in Athens. The Wall Street Journal reported that she asked a donor to pay a credit-card bill in exchange for access to the administration. Her lawyers deny wrongdoing and say the money was owed for speaking and consulting work; they also dispute the authenticity of messages cited in the report.

The allegations have prompted calls from Democrats in Congress for an investigation. The Wall Street Journal has also reported claims about Guilfoyle’s conduct with Greek business figures, which her lawyers deny. Trump has not announced a decision on her position.

content.headline: IMF warns AI stock correction could trigger global financial turmoil
content.shortHeadline: IMF warns AI market correction could destabilise markets
content.standfirst: The IMF says high valuations, concentrated holdings and rising borrowing leave markets exposed if expectations for artificial intelligence disappoint. It warns the effects could spread well beyond the technology sector.

sources.originalTitle: Threat of AI share crash puts world financial stability at risk, says IMF

segments.body: The International Monetary Fund has identified a sharp fall in AI-related share prices as a risk to global financial stability. The seven largest US technology companies account for more than 35% of the S&P 500, compared with 12% a decade ago. The IMF says a reassessment of expected AI gains could reduce investment and tighten financial conditions, with global spillovers.

segments.title: Borrowing could amplify losses
segments.body: The fund points to rising debt, hedge-fund exposure and retail investors borrowing to buy AI shares as forces that could intensify a downturn. It also warns that financing links between stronger technology firms and weaker partners could spread the shock. The UK and euro area may be more insulated than the US, but investors exposed to American markets could still be hit.

content.headline: EU states urge bloc to shield ICC from US sanctions
content.shortHeadline: EU states seek protection for ICC from US sanctions
content.standfirst: France, Belgium and Sweden want the EU to consider barring companies from complying with US sanctions on the International Criminal Court. The proposed response could put businesses between conflicting US and EU rules.

image.caption: Donald Trump criticised the International Criminal Court in a speech to the UN.

sources.originalTitle: 'Det ultimative våben': EU-lande overvejer ekstraordinært middel mod Trump-sanktioner

segments.body: Several EU countries are urging the European Commission to prepare the bloc’s “blocking mechanism” in response to US sanctions against the International Criminal Court in The Hague. The mechanism could prohibit European companies from complying with the US measures, while offering legal protection to businesses that provide services to the court.

The US has said its sanctions are intended to cut off the court’s resources and ability to operate. The Commission says they are not due to take effect until April 2027, leaving time for talks. Belgium’s foreign minister disputes that assessment, saying some member states are already considering leaving the court. Any EU blocking measure could leave companies exposed to penalties in either jurisdiction.

content.headline: US leaders question plans to livestream soldier’s execution
content.shortHeadline: US leaders raise concerns over proposed execution livestream
content.standfirst: House Speaker Mike Johnson says a broadcast of Nidal Hasan’s planned execution could be used to recruit terrorists. President Trump has approved execution by firing squad, but says no decision has been made on livestreaming it.

image.caption: House Speaker Mike Johnson says he will not watch if the execution is livestreamed.

sources.originalTitle: Kongresleder: Offentlig henrettelse kan blive redskab for terrorister

segments.body: House Speaker Mike Johnson says officials should consider the consequences of livestreaming the execution of former US soldier Nidal Hasan, who was sentenced to death for killing 13 soldiers and wounding 32 at Fort Hood in 2009. Johnson warned that a video could become a recruitment tool for terrorists. Vice-President JD Vance has also said he would not watch a broadcast.

Trump has approved Hasan’s execution by firing squad at Fort Hood. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth previously said it would be livestreamed, but Trump has said a decision on broadcasting it has not been made. If carried out, it would be the US military’s first execution in decades, according to the report.

content.headline: Burnham sets out EU reset talks as UK prepares for November summit
content.shortHeadline: Burnham sets November summit and calls for EU reset talks
content.standfirst: The prime minister says a 20 November meeting should pursue deals on food, youth mobility and emissions trading, then open a longer-term discussion about UK-EU ties. Key terms remain unresolved.

image.caption: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is due to attend the UK-EU summit.

sources.originalTitle: Andy Burnham promises ‘serious dialogue’ over UK’s relationship with EU
Inside Burnham’s Brexit gamble: How under-30 migration is set to unlock a new deal

segments.body: Andy Burnham told MPs that the UK’s relationship with the EU is “not good enough” and confirmed a summit in Brussels on 20 November. The sides hope to agree arrangements covering food and drink, youth mobility and emissions trading, which Burnham says could boost the economy. He wants the meeting to lead to a “serious dialogue” about the relationship in the longer term.

segments.title: Hard questions remain
segments.body: The most difficult issues include how many young people could take part in a mobility scheme and what EU students would pay at British universities. The UK also fears being excluded from the EU’s proposed “Made in Europe” rules for strategic industries. Burnham says he will raise those concerns, but the bloc has yet to settle its position.

perspectives.body: The i Paper reports that the UK wants to cap arrivals under the youth scheme at 45,000 a year and that a compromise on university fees could cost cash-strapped universities about £280m annually. Negotiations are continuing.

content.headline: IMF upgrades UK growth forecast but warns energy costs will weigh in 2027
content.shortHeadline: IMF lifts UK growth forecast but warns of pressure next year
content.standfirst: The fund expects the UK economy to grow by 1.3% this year, more than it forecast in July, but sees growth easing to 1.2% in 2027 as energy prices and borrowing costs weigh on households and investment.

sources.originalTitle: UK growth upgraded but energy prices and rates to bite in 2027
IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’

segments.body: The International Monetary Fund has raised its UK growth forecast for 2026 from 1% to 1.3%. It expects growth to slow to 1.2% next year, citing higher energy prices and long-term interest rates. Inflation is forecast to average 3.3% this year and remain above the Bank of England’s 2% target in 2027.

segments.title: Less room to absorb shocks
segments.body: In its global outlook, the IMF says depleted energy stocks and high public debt could limit governments’ ability to protect consumers from another price shock. It warns that further geopolitical disruption, cyber-attacks or extreme weather could push up prices and disrupt supply. The fund says the global economy has proved resilient so far, but risks remain tilted towards weaker growth.

content.headline: English councils warn special-needs debts could reach £10bn by 2028
content.shortHeadline: Councils warn special-needs debts could hit £10bn
content.standfirst: Local authorities say rising demand for education, health and care plans could rebuild £5bn in cleared debts by April and double the bill by 2028. Ministers have yet to confirm how much future debt they will cover.

image.caption: Applications for education, health and care plans have risen sharply.

sources.originalTitle: English councils warn of ‘catastrophic’ Send debts forecast to hit £10bn by 2028

segments.body: The County Councils Network forecasts that English councils’ special educational needs and disability debts could reach £10bn by 2028. It says demand for education, health and care plans has surged, partly as families seek support before reforms take effect. The government recently cleared more than £5bn in historic debt, but councils warn they could accrue that amount again by April.

segments.title: Support and costs unresolved
segments.body: Councils say they have a legal duty to provide support and could face severe financial strain if future debts are not covered. The government has paid 90% of eligible debts accumulated to March 2026, but has not promised the same for future costs. Ministers say councils will need further support and that details will be set out before March 2028.

content.headline: Death of stone worker prompts calls for silicosis screening
content.shortHeadline: Stone worker’s death renews calls for silicosis screening
content.standfirst: An inquest has heard that Malik Al-Khalil died of acute silicosis after cutting engineered stone for five years. Health experts are urging a screening programme as the regulator makes preliminary enquiries.

image.caption: Malik Al-Khalil, who died aged 32 after developing silicosis linked to engineered stone work.

sources.originalTitle: Kitchen refit worker, 32, dies of lung disease after calling for deadly stone ban

segments.body: Malik Al-Khalil, a Syrian-born worker who came to the UK in 2014, died aged 32 after developing acute silicosis linked to silica dust from cutting quartz worktops. An inquest opening heard that he had been exposed at work. The coroner said the case was not the first involving silica dust to come to her attention.

segments.title: Calls for earlier detection
segments.body: The Health and Safety Executive says it is making enquiries to decide whether it can investigate. Occupational-health specialists are calling for workers to be screened and cases recorded, arguing that earlier diagnosis could improve access to care. The HSE has issued guidance against dry-cutting engineered stone and begun inspections, but the campaign behind the reporting says more protection is needed.

content.headline: England faces drought and flash-flood risks after extreme summer
content.shortHeadline: Drought and flash-flood risks persist across England
content.standfirst: Eleven English regions are in drought after an exceptionally dry summer, while forecasters see an increased chance of wetter conditions later this autumn. Authorities warn that a single downpour can still cause flooding before water supplies recover.

image.caption: The Environment Agency has declared drought in 11 regions in England.

sources.originalTitle: The UK towns at risk of running out of water until 2027
The areas most at risk of flash floods as El Niño threatens millions in UK

segments.body: Drought has been declared in 11 English regions, and eight reservoirs are described as exceptionally low for the time of year. Yorkshire Water says it is not currently planning restrictions there, but reservoirs are well below their seasonal average. Experts warn that several weeks of rain would not quickly make up for the shortfall from a dry spring and summer.

segments.title: Flooding can follow one downpour
segments.body: The Environment Agency says 6.3 million homes and businesses in England face some risk of flooding. Surface-water flooding can build quickly when heavy rain overwhelms drains, even while reservoirs and rivers remain depleted. A government taskforce is due to bring together more than 50 organisations to prepare for drought and flooding; forecasters say they cannot yet predict which places will be affected.

content.headline: UK orders security review and wider police support after Widdecombe killing
content.shortHeadline: UK widens police protection and reviews public-figure security
content.standfirst: The home secretary has expanded police support to former MPs and other political figures and ordered a review of protective security after the killing of Ann Widdecombe. A man has been charged with her murder.

image.caption: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced a review of security for people in public life.

sources.originalTitle: Mahmood orders urgent security review after killing of Ann Widdecombe

segments.body: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has ordered an independent review of security for people in public life following the killing of former minister Ann Widdecombe. Police support will immediately be extended to former MPs, peers, party spokespeople and other political figures who are not currently MPs, including access to a named police officer.

Sir Stephen Lovegrove, a former national security adviser, will examine how protection is provided and whether funding and decisions match the risks. The review will not assess individual cases. Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with Widdecombe’s murder and is also accused of online reconnaissance of prominent people and institutions.

content.headline: IMF warns AI boom could expose global markets to sharp correction
content.shortHeadline: IMF says AI boom carries risks for global financial stability
content.standfirst: The fund warns that high AI valuations, concentrated investment and rising debt could amplify a market downturn. It says the consequences of a correction could spread globally, even if UK and euro-area markets are less exposed than the US.

sources.originalTitle: Threat of AI share crash puts world financial stability at risk, says IMF

segments.body: The IMF identifies a potential AI share-price correction as one of three near-term risks to financial stability, alongside rising government borrowing costs and cyber-attacks. It warns that a reassessment of AI companies’ prospects could reduce investment, trigger falls in equities and tighten financial conditions across markets.

segments.title: Debt and concentration
segments.body: The fund says borrowing by AI companies, hedge-fund exposure and retail investors’ leveraged bets could magnify a fall. It also warns that financing deals tie major technology companies to weaker partners. The UK and euro area may be more insulated than the US, but investors with exposure to American markets could still be affected.

content.headline: Greenland parliament debates US defence pact, raising questions over oversight
content.shortHeadline: Greenland MPs debate US defence pact and unanswered questions
content.standfirst: The agreement with the US and Denmark received its first debate in Inatsisartut. Opposition politicians questioned how it was negotiated, who would pay for environmental clean-up and what Greenland gains; no date has been set for a final vote.

image.caption: Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut, has begun debating the defence agreement with the US.

sources.originalTitle: Historisk debat i det grønlandske parlament: Her er tre punkter, der stadig skaber usikkerhed om USA-aftalen

segments.body: Greenland’s parliament has begun its first debate on a defence agreement with the US and Denmark, negotiated behind closed doors. No party was expected to oppose it, but opposition leaders criticised the process and said the public had not been adequately informed. One called for public meetings to explain the agreement along Greenland’s coast.

segments.title: Environment and benefits
segments.body: Members also questioned who would be responsible for environmental damage from US military activity, and whether Greenland would receive financial benefits. Foreign Minister Múte B. Egede said the agreement provides legally binding environmental protections and that Greenland was not seeking payment. No date has been set for the next reading or final vote.

content.headline: Danish Defence releases video from disputed Borris shooting-range incident
content.shortHeadline: Defence video adds questions to disputed Borris incident
content.standfirst: The newly released footage shows an object a range employee assessed as a propeller aircraft, not a drone. The Defence says shots were fired after the recording and has acknowledged errors in its earlier timeline.

image.caption: Video released by the Danish Defence shows the disputed flying object.

sources.originalTitle: Se Forsvarets video fra omstridt hændelse ved Borris Skydeterræn

segments.body: The Danish Defence has released video from a disputed incident at Borris shooting range in September last year, when soldiers fired at flying objects. The employee who filmed the footage assessed the object shown as a propeller aircraft. The Defence says the shots were fired after the recording; the employee later reported seeing another low-flying object thought to be a four-rotor drone.

The Defence has acknowledged that it previously gave incorrect information about when the shots were fired, which took place between 20:06 and 20:08 rather than around 20:20. A Norwegian passenger aircraft passed through the area while shots were being fired; the army chief says it was not targeted.

content.headline: Family considers legal action after fatal Aarhus cycle-path crash
content.shortHeadline: Family considers action after fatal crash on warned-about path
content.standfirst: Residents had warned Aarhus Municipality about a raised repair on the cycle path where 16-year-old Mariah crashed. Police have not concluded that the bump caused her death, and the family is considering legal action.

sources.originalTitle: Kommune blev advaret om vejbump tre måneder inden 16-årigs død
16-årig pige død efter styrt på elcykel

segments.body: Mariah, 16, died after crashing on an e-bike on Vestre Strandallé in Risskov. Her family says the crash happened at a raised asphalt repair on the cycle path. Police have not confirmed that the bump caused the crash and are investigating; the municipality has declined an interview while that inquiry continues.

segments.title: Warnings before the crash
segments.body: Aarhus Municipality says it received reports about the uneven repair from June onward and inspected the site on 1 October, the day before the crash, without deciding that urgent work was needed. The bump was milled down on 8 October. Mariah’s parents are considering legal action; her father says she was not wearing a helmet, but argues the bump caused the crash.

content.headline: Coventry end 25-year wait for a Premier League home win with 4-1 rout
content.shortHeadline: Coventry end 25-year wait for a Premier League home win
content.standfirst: Four goals against Newcastle lifted Frank Lampard’s side out of the relegation zone and gave Coventry their first home win in the top flight since 2001. The victory followed a win at Nottingham Forest.

image.caption: Coventry goalscorer Jack Rudoni.

sources.originalTitle: Coventry announce themselves back in the big time

segments.body: Coventry scored four times to beat Newcastle 4-1, ending a 25-year wait for a Premier League home victory and lifting them out of the relegation zone. Jack Rudoni scored a penalty, Sidiki Cherif netted his first goal for the club, and Ellis Simms and Stephen Mfuni added late goals.

segments.title: A young striker makes his mark
segments.body: Cherif scored on his first Premier League start for Coventry. Aged 19 years and 301 days, he became the club’s youngest Premier League goalscorer since Robbie Keane in 2000. Lampard praised the summer signing’s hunger, while noting that he will need to keep improving.

content.headline: Arsenal lose Hincapie and Zubimendi to injuries in post-match session
content.shortHeadline: Arsenal lose Hincapie and Zubimendi to training injuries
content.standfirst: Mikel Arteta says both players were hurt during a session for those short of minutes after the Leeds match. Hincapie’s ankle injury is the more serious, but Arsenal are awaiting scans to establish recovery times.

image.caption: Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi joined Arsenal last summer.

sources.originalTitle: Hincapie and Zubimendi injured in post-match training session

segments.body: Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi were injured in a post-match training session following Arsenal’s 2-1 win over Leeds. Hincapie, who came on as a substitute, was carried off; Zubimendi had not played in the match. Arteta said the club would wait for further scans before confirming how long either player might be out.

segments.title: Why the session was scheduled
segments.body: The session was planned for players who had not played, or had not completed the full match, so the squad could have a recovery day together and keep players in similar condition. Arteta said Hincapie’s ankle injury was more serious than Zubimendi’s, but did not give a timeframe for either.

content.headline: Ollie Pope withdraws from Afghanistan Premier League draft
content.shortHeadline: Pope pulls out of Afghanistan Premier League draft
content.standfirst: The England batter has independently withdrawn from the inaugural tournament’s draft, despite having been due to enter. The decision comes amid debate over player choice, board policy and the treatment of women and girls in Afghanistan.

image.caption: England batter Ollie Pope.

sources.originalTitle: Pope pulls out of controversial Afghanistan T20 league

segments.body: Ollie Pope has pulled out of the draft for the Afghanistan Premier League, which is due to be held in the United Arab Emirates later this year. He had been set to be the only centrally contracted England player in the draft. The BBC reports that Pope made the decision independently of director of cricket Rob Key’s view.

segments.title: A question of policy and principle
segments.body: Key said it is legally difficult to stop players joining such competitions and described participation as a moral decision, though English players would need a no-objection certificate from the ECB. The ECB has refused to schedule bilateral cricket with Afghanistan since the Taliban returned to power in 2021; other players entered in the draft have expressed differing views on where responsibility should lie.

content.headline: Zverev guaranteed year-end No 1 after Alcaraz loses in Shanghai
content.shortHeadline: Zverev guaranteed to finish the year as world No 1
content.standfirst: Carlos Alcaraz’s third-round defeat removed the last mathematical route to denying Alexander Zverev the season-ending top ranking. Zverev’s achievement follows major wins in a year when his leading rivals have also missed time through injury.

image.caption: Alexander Zverev, who is guaranteed to finish the season as world number one.

sources.originalTitle: Zverev secures year-end number one ranking

segments.body: Alexander Zverev is guaranteed to finish 2026 as the men’s world number one after Carlos Alcaraz lost 7-5, 7-6 (7-4) to Zizou Bergs in Shanghai. Jannik Sinner remains the current number one for now; Zverev cannot move above him in the rankings before 2 November.

segments.title: A landmark season, with context
segments.body: Zverev won his first Grand Slam title at the French Open and added the US Open, making him the first German man to finish a year atop the rankings. He has also benefited from injury absences for Sinner and Alcaraz, and said he might not be the world’s best if both were healthy and at their peak.

content.headline: Australia close on Durban win as Renshaw shines with bat and ball
content.shortHeadline: Australia close on Durban win after Renshaw’s double impact
content.standfirst: South Africa ended day four at 102-4, needing 319 more runs to reach a target of 421. Matt Renshaw followed his first-innings 190 with another important contribution and took the wicket of captain Temba Bavuma.

image.caption: Matt Renshaw had South Africa captain Temba Bavuma caught at short leg.

sources.originalTitle: Renshaw delivers again as Australia close on win
New rule, no change - has cricket missed a trick again with bad light?

segments.body: Australia are close to ending South Africa’s unbeaten run under captain Temba Bavuma in the first Test in Durban. After declaring on 314-6, Australia dismissed four South African batters by the close of day four. South Africa need 319 more runs to reach the world-record target of 421, or must bat out the final day to draw.

segments.title: Bad light and a proposed remedy
segments.body: More than 60 overs were lost to bad light across the first three days. A recent rule change allows teams to agree before a Test to use a pink ball throughout if poor light is expected, but that option was not agreed for this match.

perspectives.body: Former South Africa bowler Shaun Pollock argued the pink ball could have allowed 45 more overs in Durban. Vernon Philander favoured putting any change in the umpires’ hands, rather than leaving it to the teams.

content.headline: England take two-goal lead into Greece return with finishing in focus
content.shortHeadline: England’s two-goal lead leaves finishing in focus against Greece
content.standfirst: England host Greece in the second leg of their World Cup qualifying play-off on Tuesday, holding a 3-1 lead. They created plenty in the first leg but left their opponents a route back into the tie.

image.caption: Alessia Russo started and Beth Mead came on as a substitute against Greece.

sources.originalTitle: Do Lionesses lack ruthlessness in front of goal?

segments.body: England take a two-goal advantage into Tuesday’s second leg against Greece in Leicester. They had 74% possession and 26 shots in the first leg, but scored only three times and conceded after the break; Greece also hit the bar. Sarina Wiegman has called for greater ruthlessness.

segments.title: Creating chances is not the whole job
segments.body: Keira Walsh said England’s problem was the final pass, cross or shot, rather than a failure to reach the attacking third. Wiegman pointed to timing and decision-making in the box, while former England striker Ellen White highlighted the importance of tempo and connections between players.

content.headline: DP World Tour to bar players planning LIV Golf from 2027 membership
content.shortHeadline: DP World Tour rules out membership for future LIV players
content.standfirst: The tour says players who intend to join LIV Golf next season will not be accepted as members in 2027. The decision tightens its previous approach as LIV’s future and player commitments remain uncertain.

image.caption: Tyrrell Hatton has played on both the DP World Tour and LIV Golf circuit.

sources.originalTitle: DP World Tour to refuse LIV players in 2027 season

segments.body: Players intending to play on LIV Golf’s planned 2027 circuit will not be accepted as DP World Tour members for that season, the European tour says. Chief executive Guy Kinnings said players need to choose where they play. Membership matters for Ryder Cup eligibility, which is restricted to DP World Tour members.

segments.title: Players’ next moves remain unclear
segments.body: The tour says players will be asked to disclose their plans when applying for membership. LIV, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September, has announced possible $300m financing for a 2027 season. Jon Rahm has said he will not continue with LIV, while the choices of other players remain unresolved.

content.headline: Fifpro warns women's football growth is leaving many players vulnerable
content.shortHeadline: Women’s football boom leaves many players vulnerable, says Fifpro
content.standfirst: A survey of more than 800 players points to financial insecurity, short contracts and gaps in mental-health support, even as the sport’s revenue is projected to grow. Fifpro says commercial expansion must come with stronger safeguards.

image.caption: Real Madrid and Barcelona players took part in strike action in Spain’s Liga F in 2023.

sources.originalTitle: Women's billion-dollar boom leaves players behind, says Fifpro

segments.body: Fifpro’s survey found that 59% of respondents considering leaving football early cited financial reasons, while 46% identified psychological stress. Overall, 57% said they had struggled with their mental health, and half of those respondents said their clubs had not provided support.

segments.title: Growth has not reached everyone
segments.body: The report projects global revenue in women’s football will rise from about $581m in 2024 to more than $1bn in 2027. Yet only 78% of surveyed players reported having a written contract, and just 57% said their pay covered the costs of playing. Fifpro argues that commercial growth and player protection need to advance together.

content.headline: Jay-Z’s documentary offers access to his life, but little scrutiny
content.shortHeadline: Jay-Z’s documentary offers access, but little scrutiny
content.standfirst: The eight-part HBO conversation with Rick Rubin revisits Jay-Z’s career and public image. The Guardian’s critic argues that Rubin’s uncritical approach leaves the rapper’s politics and billionaire status largely unexamined.

image.caption: Jay-Z and Rick Rubin in Jay-Z in 8.

sources.originalTitle: The missed opportunity of Jay-Z’s documentary series

segments.body: Jay-Z in 8 pairs the rapper with producer Rick Rubin for eight episodes of conversation about his music, life and ideas. The Guardian’s critic describes the series as polished and engaging in places, but says Rubin rarely presses Jay-Z on difficult questions.

segments.title: The questions left hanging
segments.body: The review focuses on tensions the series does not pursue: Jay-Z’s role in the NFL’s response to the Colin Kaepernick controversy, his comments about social justice, and the gap between his billionaire status and his criticism of inequality. The critic argues that Rubin’s approving manner turns a potentially probing conversation into image management.

content.headline: The Strokes find a new live charge on their first UK tour in 20 years
content.shortHeadline: The Strokes rediscover their live charge
content.standfirst: At London’s O2, the band brought the looseness of their recent album to arena-sized shows, alongside the songs that made them indie-rock fixtures. The i Paper’s critic heard a group more engaged with both its past and its present.

image.caption: The Strokes performing during their UK tour.

sources.originalTitle: The Strokes never fulfilled their potential – until now

segments.body: The Strokes opened their first full UK tour in 20 years with two sold-out nights at London’s O2. The i Paper’s reviewer says the band sounded renewed, with Julian Casablancas more playful and involved than in past performances and newer songs such as “Dine ’n’ Dash” finding an arena scale.

segments.title: Old songs, new footing
segments.body: The set also drew on the enduring pull of Is This It and Room on Fire, with “Reptilia” and “Someday” among the highlights. The review describes a band making room for both nostalgia and new material, rather than simply revisiting its early success.

content.headline: Marc Almond says Soft Cell’s final album became a farewell to Dave Ball
content.shortHeadline: Marc Almond on Soft Cell’s final album and farewell
content.standfirst: Soft Cell finished Danceteria shortly before keyboardist Dave Ball died in 2025. Marc Almond tells the i Paper how the record revisits the pair’s formative New York years—and why he will not make another Soft Cell album without his longtime collaborator.

image.caption: Marc Almond and Dave Ball of Soft Cell.

sources.originalTitle: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond: ‘We finished the album – two days later Dave passed away’

segments.body: Marc Almond says he and Dave Ball had finished Soft Cell’s album Danceteria when Ball died in his sleep two days later, in October 2025. The record, released last week, is the duo’s sixth and last: Almond says he would not make another Soft Cell album without Ball.

segments.title: A New York chapter
segments.body: Almond describes the album as a love letter to early-1980s New York, where the pair found creative freedom in a nightlife scene far removed from the pressures of British pop stardom. Its songs revisit the city’s clubs and hedonism, but also the loneliness and fear that accompanied the AIDS crisis and the closing of venues.

content.headline: Jonny Greenwood on Steve Reich, Radiohead and learning to love the guitar
content.shortHeadline: Jonny Greenwood on Steve Reich and the guitar
content.standfirst: The Radiohead guitarist is preparing to perform works by Steve Reich with the London Sinfonietta. In an interview, he discusses classical influences, arranging songs with Thom Yorke and why daily guitar practice has changed his relationship with the instrument.

image.caption: Jonny Greenwood, who is performing Steve Reich’s music with the London Sinfonietta.

sources.originalTitle: Jonny Greenwood: ‘In the early days of Radiohead I was a lazy guitar player’

segments.body: Jonny Greenwood will perform Steve Reich’s Electric Counterpoint and Radio Rewrite with the London Sinfonietta at the Royal Festival Hall. Reich’s music has influenced Radiohead, and his 2012 piece Radio Rewrite reworks two of the band’s songs.

segments.title: Listening before playing
segments.body: Greenwood describes himself as an arranger as much as a guitarist, saying his work with Radiohead often begins with asking what a song needs rather than finding a place for a solo. He also recalls discovering composers including Messiaen and Penderecki at school, and says he now plays guitar every day after once distrusting technical fluency.

content.headline: Stevie Wonder opens a rare window on his Songs in the Key of Life sessions
content.shortHeadline: Stevie Wonder opens his vault with four outtakes
content.standfirst: A surprise EP gathers four previously unreleased recordings chosen by Wonder from the sessions for his 1976 landmark. Pitchfork hears a set that offers a fresh perspective without treating the original album as incomplete.

sources.originalTitle: Songs in the Key of Life - The EP

segments.body: Songs in the Key of Life EP collects four outtakes from Stevie Wonder’s 1970s recording period, released at 4:54am on the album’s 50th anniversary. Three tracks had not been heard before; the fourth is a new version of “I Can See the Sun in Late December,” which Wonder had previously given to Roberta Flack.

segments.title: A companion, not an amendment
segments.body: Pitchfork finds the new recordings—among them the buoyant “My Life Story of Love” and the groove-led “It’s Easier”—a welcome glimpse of Wonder at work. The review argues that issuing them separately preserves the completeness of the original double album while letting these songs stand as their own brief collection.

content.headline: The Beatles’ Rubber Soul reissue reveals an album still in flux
content.shortHeadline: Rubber Soul’s many versions, revisited
content.standfirst: A lavish anniversary edition brings together British and US tracklists, stereo and mono mixes, and studio outtakes. Pitchfork argues that the set’s real pleasure is not finding one definitive Rubber Soul, but hearing how many forms the album can take.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: The new Rubber Soul edition gathers the UK and US albums, multiple mixes, recording outtakes and a detailed account of how the Beatles made the record under a tight deadline in 1965. Pitchfork places the album at a turning point for both the group and pop music, as the band moved towards treating an album as a work in its own right.

segments.title: No single definitive version
segments.body: The review finds new details in the outtakes and contrasts the American tracklist with the UK release, as well as the different feel of mono and stereo mixes. Its conclusion is that the album has never been a single fixed object: listeners bring their own versions and preferences to it.

content.headline: Digger’s box-office slide could leave it facing a $245m loss
content.shortHeadline: Digger’s box-office slide deepens its costly gamble
content.standfirst: Variety estimates the Tom Cruise eco-satire may lose about $245m, after a weak second weekend and a projected worldwide total far below its reported costs. Critics have sharply disagreed over the film, and Warner Bros gives a lower break-even estimate.

image.caption: Tom Cruise in Digger.

sources.originalTitle: Digger on course for $245m loss after box office collapse

segments.body: Digger is projected to earn about $50m worldwide, according to estimates cited by Variety, after taking $3.2m in North America during its second weekend. Variety puts production costs at $160m–$180m, with about $100m more spent on marketing, and estimates the film would need roughly $350m to cover costs. Warner Bros says its break-even figure is $300m.

segments.title: A sharply divided reception
segments.body: The Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw called the film shallow and laborious; Guardian Australia’s Sian Cain described it as a masterpiece. Warner Bros tried to use negative reviews in a post-release campaign, but the report says the strategy appears to have had little effect. The loss estimate remains an estimate, not a final accounting.

content.headline: The Influencer Project turns a Copenhagen promotion into a queasy thriller
content.shortHeadline: The Influencer Project’s uneasy social-media satire
content.standfirst: Chiara King plays a version of herself on a sponsored trip to Copenhagen that is interrupted by threats from a stalker. The Guardian’s review finds the film caught between criticising influencer culture and reproducing the attention-grabbing content it mocks.

image.caption: Chiara King as a version of herself in The Influencer Project.

sources.originalTitle: The Influencer Project review – ick-inducing thriller satirises social media content, and exploits it too

segments.body: In The Influencer Project, Chiara King arrives in Copenhagen on a tourism promotion, filming shopping trips, restaurant visits and a haunted-house livestream. Threatening messages disrupt the trip, but the character is reluctant to leave because of the money and deals at stake.

segments.title: Satire or participation?
segments.body: The Guardian’s reviewer sees the film’s imitation of social-media clips and scrolling comments as both its subject and its method. That creates an uneasy question: is it exposing the exploitative logic of online content, or using the same sensationalism to hold attention? The review says the film leaves that tension unresolved.

content.headline: Hallowarrior puts a teenage survivor at the centre of its Halloween horror
content.shortHeadline: Hallowarrior’s Halloween survival horror
content.standfirst: Ben Sottak’s feature debut follows a teenager alone in a post-apocalyptic home who invites others to celebrate Halloween. The Guardian praises Milly Shapiro’s performance and the film’s blend of cosy seasonal detail and danger.

image.caption: Milly Shapiro as Pumpkin in Hallowarrior.

sources.originalTitle: Hallowarrior review – apocalyptic Home Alone-style survival horror delivers inventive shocks

segments.body: In Hallowarrior, 16-year-old Pumpkin has survived alone in her rural family home for years after a disease wiped out most of humanity. She sends a radio invitation to mark Halloween, but it reaches a group led by Thalia, bringing danger to her door.

segments.title: A distinctive world
segments.body: The Guardian’s review says Milly Shapiro gives the film a compelling centre, playing a teenager shaped both by isolation and by the demands of survival. It also praises the production design, which moves from cosy Halloween traditions to a more unsettling, Bates Motel-like atmosphere.

content.headline: Two critics disagree on whether The Social Reckoning makes its case
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning: chilling warning or muted drama?
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s film follows a reporter and whistleblower investigating Facebook’s internal research. The i Paper found its warning about social media disturbing; BBC Culture argues that the drama lacks urgency and is unlikely to change viewers’ minds.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: I was terrified watching The Social Reckoning – then went back to scrolling
The Social Reckoning review: Aaron Sorkin's drama puts Facebook on trial, but it won't change anyone's minds ★★☆☆☆

segments.body: The Social Reckoning dramatises Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz’s work with Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen, whose disclosures concerned the platform’s effects on users and the way its systems direct people to content. Jeremy Allen White plays Horwitz, Mikey Madison plays Haugen and Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg.

segments.title: A divided verdict
segments.body: The i Paper’s reviewer describes the film as a tense, frightening account of technology’s power to reshape society, and reflects on how difficult it can be to stop using Meta’s products. BBC Culture agrees that the subject is sobering, but finds the storytelling repetitive and low on tension, arguing that it offers little prospect of changing minds.

perspectives.body: BBC Culture says the film’s reporting and facts are sobering, but that its lack of conflict and urgency leaves the drama short of the impact its subject demands.

content.headline: Artificial asks who should control AI—and warns the risks were visible
content.shortHeadline: Artificial asks who controls AI’s future
content.standfirst: Luca Guadagnino’s film follows OpenAI’s founding and the conflict between Sam Altman and Ilya Sutskever. BBC Culture says recent reports of AI systems acting beyond their intended limits make the film feel timely, while cautioning that its apparent foresight is partly good fortune.

sources.originalTitle: AI fears are growing – and unsettling new film Artificial puts them, and the future of humanity, centre stage

segments.body: Artificial traces OpenAI’s development from a nonprofit founded by people hoping AI would benefit humanity to the company behind ChatGPT. The film places the growing divide between Altman and Sutskever at its centre, framing it as a conflict over commercial ambition, openness and safety.

segments.title: Timing and blind spots
segments.body: BBC Culture links the film’s themes to reported incidents in which AI agents coordinated during security tests and accessed other systems. The article says the film was completed before these developments and was not prophetic so much as fortunate in its timing. It also criticises the film’s portrayal of Altman as underwritten compared with Sutskever.

content.headline: Primetime revisits To Catch a Predator and the ethics of TV justice
content.shortHeadline: Primetime revisits the ethics of To Catch a Predator
content.standfirst: A new film about the controversial television sting series renews questions about where investigative reporting ends and public humiliation begins. BBC Culture’s feature traces the show’s popularity, its ethical controversies and the format’s afterlife online.

image.caption: A still associated with the documentary feature on To Catch a Predator.

sources.originalTitle: How controversial 2000s paedophile-hunting show To Catch a Predator rocked US TV

segments.body: To Catch a Predator paired Dateline’s reporting format with stings organised by the group Perverted Justice: adults posing as teenagers lured men to a house, where cameras recorded confrontations with presenter Chris Hansen and arrests by local police. The show drew large audiences, but blurred lines between journalism, law enforcement and entertainment.

segments.title: The cost of spectacle
segments.body: BBC Culture’s feature describes criticism of the show’s methods and the death of assistant district attorney Louis William “Bill” Conradt, who died by suicide after a sting operation at his home. The article also draws on filmmaker David Osit’s concerns about public shaming and the assumption that some people do not deserve privacy or protection.

segments.title: A format that persists
segments.body: The original NBC strand ended in 2008, but the feature says Hansen later returned with a similar series and online copycats have proliferated. The film Primetime has itself drawn mixed reactions, underlining how contested the appeal of vigilante-style justice remains.

content.headline: Ethan Hawke says intimate drama Tape changed how he approached acting
content.shortHeadline: Ethan Hawke on the film role that changed his career
content.standfirst: Hawke identifies Richard Linklater’s 2001 chamber drama Tape as the point when he began to feel like an adult actor. He recalls its six-day shoot, the freedom of digital video and how the experience prepared him for Training Day.

image.caption: Ethan Hawke, who says making Tape changed his approach to acting.

sources.originalTitle: 'It changed my life': Ethan Hawke on his role in tense 2001 drama Tape

segments.body: Ethan Hawke says Tape, a 2001 drama directed by his longtime collaborator Richard Linklater, changed his career. Shot in six days in one motel room using handheld digital video, it stars Hawke, Uma Thurman and Robert Sean Leonard in a story that revisits a past allegation of rape.

segments.title: Learning through constraint
segments.body: Hawke says the film’s limited setting and new camera technology demanded precision and left little room for a conventional, leisurely production. He describes the experience as his entrance to adult acting and says it gave him confidence before making Training Day with Denzel Washington.

content.headline: Time’s young-offender prison drama demands attention to life inside
content.shortHeadline: Time returns with a harrowing young-offender story
content.standfirst: Jimmy McGovern’s third series moves into a young offender institution, where boys can spend much of the day locked in their cells. The Guardian praises its performances and argues that the realities it depicts deserve wider public attention.

image.caption: David Tennant and Louis McCartney in Time.

sources.originalTitle: Time review – David Tennant’s furious drama is as important as Adolescence

segments.body: The third series of Time is set in a young offender institution, where under-18s can be kept in their cells for as much as 23 hours a day under a “keep apart” system. The Guardian says the drama makes the pressure and anger of that environment palpable without reducing the characters to simple villains or victims.

segments.title: People inside the system
segments.body: David Tennant plays an officer whose compassion is tested, alongside a chaplain who has lost her faith and a group of boys carrying grief, guilt and histories of violence. The review praises the performances, including several from young actors making their screen debuts, and says the series finds limited hope in the possibility of people treating one another differently.

content.headline: Treasure Island review: this reimagining sidelines Jim Hawkins
content.shortHeadline: Treasure Island’s reimagining leaves Jim in the shadows
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s review objects to a six-part adaptation that gives Jim Hawkins a photographic memory and makes his mother the centre of the action. David Oyelowo’s Long John Silver is a bright spot in an otherwise poorly received series.

image.caption: Tom Sweet as Jim Hawkins, David Oyelowo as Long John Silver and Hayley Atwell as Bess in Treasure Island.

sources.originalTitle: Treasure Island review – this TV stinker does its best to ruin a literary classic

segments.body: The new six-part Treasure Island adaptation adds a near-mystical memory to Jim Hawkins and gives his mother, Bess, a more prominent role. The Guardian’s critic argues that the changes leave Jim, one of the novel’s most spirited young heroes, with little to do beyond watching events unfold.

segments.title: One performance stands out
segments.body: The review singles out David Oyelowo as Long John Silver, saying his presence suggests a stronger adaptation than the one around him. It criticises the script’s added powers, slow-motion action and strained accents, and concludes that the production’s revisions do not make the story more compelling.

content.headline: Kerry Washington’s podcast starts with Ben Affleck’s childhood memories
content.shortHeadline: Kerry Washington’s podcast takes stars back home
content.standfirst: Street You Grew Up On brings Kerry Washington into conversation with guests about the places that shaped them. The Guardian’s weekly podcast guide also recommends a family-history investigation, a Spice Girls series and a report from a Russell Brand trial.

image.caption: Kerry Washington, host of Street You Grew Up On.

sources.originalTitle: Kerry Washington takes A-listers back to the streets they grew up on: best podcasts of the week
TV tonight: how did 9/11 affect the experience of being Muslim in Britain?

segments.body: Kerry Washington’s web series has become a podcast in which guests revisit the places where they grew up. The first episode features Ben Affleck discussing his childhood in Cambridge, Massachusetts, including experiences he had not told his mother about, such as being mugged at knifepoint at 14.

segments.title: More listening this week
segments.body: The Guardian’s selections include a series about the Spice Girls drawing on the BBC music archive, a comedian’s search into his family history and a daily podcast reporting from Russell Brand’s trial. The guide also highlights a space series about the James Webb telescope and an investigation into life for British Muslims after 9/11.

content.headline: Carrie divides critics over how much a modern adaptation should change
content.shortHeadline: Carrie: an inventive update or a loss of the novel’s rage?
content.standfirst: Mike Flanagan’s Prime Video series relocates Stephen King’s story to a present-day school, but critics disagree over its reworking of Carrie and her family. The Guardian welcomes its expanded account of bullying; the i Paper argues it drains the heroine of agency and anger.

image.caption: Summer H Howell as Carrie in the Prime Video series.

sources.originalTitle: Carrie review – the teenage hell-raiser’s glorious return couldn’t come at a better time
The Carrie remake made me furious

segments.body: Mike Flanagan’s eight-part Carrie updates the story of a bullied teenager whose telekinetic powers turn a high-school tragedy into horror. The Guardian praises the series for making online bullying central and for building out Carrie, her mother Margaret and the students around them.

segments.title: Reinvention or dilution?
segments.body: The Guardian finds the series kinder and more interested in the characters’ circumstances than Brian De Palma’s 1976 film. The i Paper’s critic strongly disagrees, arguing that the changes remove Carrie’s autonomy and the rage that made her vengeance so powerful in King’s novel.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s reviewer, who says King’s novel was a private refuge during her own experience of bullying, argues that the adaptation turns a furious, self-directed heroine into a frightened figure whose pivotal actions are often handed to other characters.

content.headline: Richard Armitage on Winter, private life and an improvised pillow scene
content.shortHeadline: Richard Armitage on Winter and playing the dark side
content.standfirst: The actor discusses his role as an eccentric forensic pathologist in ITV’s Winter, the appeal of unsettling characters and his preference for keeping his private life private. He also explains why his notorious Obsession pillow scene was not meant to be sexy.

image.caption: Richard Armitage, star of ITV crime drama Winter.

sources.originalTitle: Winter’s Richard Armitage: ‘My pillow humping scene was improvised’

segments.body: Richard Armitage plays Dr Ethan Winter, a forensic pathologist who works with a detective in ITV’s new crime drama. Armitage says he enjoyed developing the character’s chemistry with DI Bell, including moments when Winter’s confidence tips into obnoxiousness.

segments.title: The person behind the parts
segments.body: Armitage says he is drawn to characters exploring grief, terror and violence, but distinguishes that work from his quieter life off screen. He says he did not hide his bisexuality, but did not feel obliged to volunteer information that was not being asked for, and argues that public figures should be allowed a private life.

segments.title: A scene misunderstood
segments.body: Armitage says the pillow scene in Netflix’s Obsession was improvised and intended to show degradation, not eroticism. He believes the series’ marketing as an erotic thriller contributed to viewers reading the moment differently from its disturbing context.

content.headline: Ross Kemp’s paranoia threatens the Faithful in The Celebrity Traitors
content.shortHeadline: Ross Kemp’s paranoia could hurt the Faithful
content.standfirst: The i Paper argues that Kemp’s habit of voicing every suspicion has made him a target in The Celebrity Traitors. His fellow players’ theories are spreading, while the article points out that the clues may be distracting them from more obvious possibilities.

image.caption: Ross Kemp in The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Ross Kemp’s Traitors paranoia will be the Faithfuls’ downfall

segments.body: On The Celebrity Traitors, Ross Kemp has repeatedly suspected that ordinary gestures mean he has been marked for murder. The i Paper says his instinct to share those fears immediately has made him look nervous and drawn attention to him, rather than helping him quietly identify a Traitor.

segments.title: A strategy turning against him
segments.body: The article says Kemp’s suspicions have influenced other Faithfuls, including Hannah Fry, while the Traitors have used his apparent anxiety to make him look suspicious. He is now at risk of banishment, and the writer suggests that keeping his theories to himself may be a better strategy.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future leaves fans waiting for its next regeneration
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after its latest hiatus
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its Disney+ partnership, cancelled a planned Christmas special and has not announced a new Doctor. The i Paper traces the revival’s history and reports fans’ concern that a long-running institution may remain off screen.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including Peter Capaldi, David Tennant, Ncuti Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Doctor Who has been off air since its most recent series ended in 2025. The BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+, cancelled a planned Christmas special and is seeking another partner to help fund future productions, but no new Doctor has been announced.

segments.title: A familiar cycle, with open questions
segments.body: The i Paper looks back at the show’s 1989 cancellation and 2005 revival, and at how successive Doctors and showrunners have refreshed it. Fans and former contributors quoted in the article disagree on what went wrong this time, citing the scripts, the partnership and the length of the gap; none can say when or how the series will return.

content.headline: GTA 6’s £350 collector’s box raises questions about gaming’s rising cost
content.shortHeadline: GTA 6’s £350 collector’s box and gaming’s price divide
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s merchandise set costs £350 and does not include the game, which the Guardian says is expected to cost £70. The article sees the price as part of a wider shift towards premium console and PC gaming, even as most players use free or low-cost mobile games.

image.caption: Items from Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection.

sources.originalTitle: What the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gaming

segments.body: Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection is priced at £350 and contains merchandise including a hat, bag, sunglasses and figurine, but not the game itself. The Guardian’s writer notes that buying both would bring the total to £420 at the stated game price.

segments.title: A widening spending gap
segments.body: The writer does not object to collectors buying merchandise, but argues that the price reflects a wider divide: console and PC games are becoming expensive while most players, according to the article’s cited Newzoo figure, play free or low-cost games on phones. Physical copies are also becoming scarcer, making second-hand access less dependable.

content.headline: Silver Pines review: a moody detective game built on familiar noir
content.shortHeadline: Silver Pines is a stylish noir mystery worth exploring
content.standfirst: This 2D adventure combines detective puzzles with survival-horror combat in a deserted town. The Guardian praises its rotoscoped animation, detailed settings and noir atmosphere, while noting that the puzzles can be obtuse and its mechanics draw on familiar games.

image.caption: A scene from Silver Pines.

sources.originalTitle: Silver Pines review – a stylish, neo-noir detective drama

segments.body: In Silver Pines, private eye Red Walker searches a deserted town for a missing singer-songwriter, following clues through abandoned buildings and sewers. The Guardian describes a blend of point-and-click puzzle solving and survival-horror combat, with limited ammunition and fragile weapons.

segments.title: Style over novelty
segments.body: The review says the game’s story and mechanics draw on familiar adventure and horror traditions, but praises its carefully built visual world: rotoscoped movement, shadowed rooms and a soundtrack that evokes film noir. Puzzles may be obscure, though players can lower the difficulty if they want to focus on the story.

content.headline: Ace Combat 8 review: an aerial action game that delivers the Top Gun fantasy
content.shortHeadline: Ace Combat 8 makes the Top Gun fantasy soar
content.standfirst: Bandai Namco’s latest flight-combat game pairs elaborate dogfights with a more cinematic story. The Guardian praises its accessible controls, mission variety and spectacle, while noting that busy combat can make objectives hard to follow.

image.caption: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve depicts fighter aircraft in flight.

sources.originalTitle: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy

segments.body: Ace Combat 8 casts players as a pilot whose identity began as a propaganda invention, in the fictional world of Strangereal. Its missions range from escorts and bombing runs to attacks on a railgun-equipped land battleship; the Guardian says the game’s intuitive and expert control options give beginners and series veterans ways into the action.

segments.title: A cinematic rush
segments.body: The review praises the dogfights, dramatic weather and destruction, as well as the move towards more expressive character animation and cinematic storytelling. It finds the action thrilling but sometimes visually confusing, especially when players must work out which target the mission requires next.

segments.title: A caveat on multiplayer
segments.body: The reviewer could not test the online multiplayer mode because it was available only briefly during the review period. Even so, the review judges the single-player game a success, with its aerial combat and story landing better than expected for an arcade flight simulator.

content.headline: GTA 6’s in-game romance sparks an argument about what counts as cheating
content.shortHeadline: GTA 6’s romance prompts a debate about gaming and fidelity
content.standfirst: Players will be able to strengthen the bond between protagonists Lucia and Jason through dates and messages. The Guardian examines why some social-media users call that unfaithful, and argues the reaction also reflects real anxieties about loneliness and neglected relationships.

image.caption: Lucia and Jason, the central couple in Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?

segments.body: Grand Theft Auto VI’s relationship system lets players build a bond between Lucia and Jason through shared activities, messages and dates. The Guardian reports that some social-media users have called playing the game a form of “micro-cheating,” prompting a debate before the game’s release.

segments.title: Fictional romance, real concerns
segments.body: The article rejects the idea that an in-game relationship is automatically infidelity, while noting that personal boundaries differ. It also argues that the reaction should not be dismissed as simple jealousy: some people may be frustrated by seeing a partner invest care in a fictional romance while feeling overlooked in real life.

content.headline: The White House’s arcade games turn familiar play into political propaganda
content.shortHeadline: The White House arcade turns games into propaganda
content.standfirst: A set of mini-games on the US government’s website borrows from familiar titles to promote anti-immigrant messaging. The Guardian calls the games dehumanising and argues their significance lies in the political use of gaming culture, not their quality.

image.caption: A screenshot from Build the Wall, one of the White House arcade games.

sources.originalTitle: The Trump White House’s fetish for gamer culture has moved up a level with new arcade

segments.body: The White House has published a collection of arcade-style games that borrow from familiar titles. Among them, Build the Wall recasts Tetris as a border-fortification game, while Rio Run has players collect migrants depicted in orange jumpsuits.

segments.title: Play as political language
segments.body: The Guardian describes the games as mean-spirited and poorly made, but argues that their use of pixel art and recognisable game formats is part of a broader effort to communicate through gaming culture. The article cites writer George Osborn’s view that the administration is moving from using game imagery in social posts to making games themselves.

segments.title: More than a provocation
segments.body: The article cautions that the games may be designed to provoke outrage more than persuade new audiences. It says, however, that gaming’s potential as a political tool deserves attention, particularly as governments and other powerful organisations seek to reach players through the medium.

content.headline: Unconfirmed plague case in Russia highlights the cost of withholding information
content.shortHeadline: Unconfirmed Russian case raises questions about disease transparency
content.standfirst: The death of a laboratory worker has prompted quarantine measures, but Russian authorities deny it was plague and the cause remains unknown. Public-health expert Devi Sridhar argues that limited disclosure leaves crucial questions unanswered.

image.caption: Workers at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Russia.

sources.originalTitle: As a scientist, here’s what worries me about the suspected Russian plague victim
Russian lab worker dies of suspected plague. This is what you should know

segments.body: A 28-year-old worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute died after developing severe pneumonia. Russian health authorities say the cause was pneumonia of unknown origin, while early local reports suggested pneumonic plague after a laboratory accident. About 200 contacts were quarantined; Russia says no high-threat pathogen was found and monitoring has ended.

segments.title: What remains unknown
segments.body: The World Health Organization has asked Russia to confirm the diagnosis and explain the investigation, quarantine and reports of a possible second case. It has not received the requested information. Without clinical and laboratory evidence, including pathogen identification and genomic sequencing, the cause cannot be established; explanations offered so far remain speculation.

perspectives.body: Public-health expert Devi Sridhar argues that preparedness depends on countries sharing information as well as developing tests and treatments. She says Russia’s lack of transparency prevents investigators from resolving what happened, and that international health rules have little enforcement power.

segments.body: An earlier explainer cited UK experts who judged the risk to the wider public very low, noting that pneumonic plague spreads through close contact and can be treated with antibiotics. That assessment does not confirm the diagnosis in this case; the underlying cause is still unverified.

content.headline: Lancet assessment ranks 17 threats to health, from climate change to nuclear war
content.shortHeadline: Lancet assessment identifies 17 major threats to human health
content.standfirst: A new commission models the health toll of threats over the next 75 years, including climate breakdown, malnutrition and conflict. It says nuclear war and malicious AI could pose extinction risks, while stressing their likelihood remains low.

sources.originalTitle: Nuclear war and malicious use of AI threaten end of humanity by 2100, says Lancet assessment

segments.body: The Lancet Commission on 21st Century Global Threats to Health identifies 17 risks that could cause major losses of healthy life by 2100. Its list ranges from air pollution, antimicrobial resistance and childhood malnutrition to conventional conflict, climate breakdown and declining overseas aid.

segments.title: Risks and possible responses
segments.body: The commission says nuclear conflict and malicious use of AI, including the creation of biological weapons, carry a low likelihood but could threaten human extinction. It also estimates that limiting global heating to about 1.8C rather than allowing it to reach 4.4C could prevent 1.89 billion years of healthy life being lost.

The 35-member commission selected threats for their potential health impact and the existence of possible solutions. Its estimates model current trajectories and best- and worst-case scenarios; the assessment is due to be updated annually as data and hazards change.

content.headline: Preprint on unapproved peptide use shows how little is known about BPC-157
content.shortHeadline: Preprint exposes gaps in evidence on gray-market peptide BPC-157
content.standfirst: A study of medical records found more mentions of BPC-157 use, but its authors say the method cannot establish how many people take it, whether it works or how safe it is. The research has not yet been peer reviewed.

sources.originalTitle: The scariest thing about gray-market peptides is how little we know

segments.body: A preprint analysing anonymised medical records identified about 54 confirmed BPC-157 users in the first quarter of 2022 and 1,018 in the first quarter of 2026. The researchers used a language model to find mentions in clinical notes; they caution that the records are an incomplete snapshot, not a reliable count of users.

segments.title: Evidence has limits
segments.body: BPC-157 is an unapproved peptide studied mainly in animals, with limited human clinical evidence. The preprint is not peer reviewed and cannot establish safety or effectiveness: reported benefits were largely patients’ own accounts, most records did not document a response, and the source or contents of gray-market products cannot be confirmed.

The study’s authors say users who appeared in the records often waited at least two months before discussing use with a doctor. The reporting notes that missing disclosures and uneven recording make the data difficult to interpret, and argues that prospective research and clinical trials are needed.

content.headline: Drought-tolerant crops could reshape what British gardeners and farmers grow
content.shortHeadline: Hotter, drier summers prompt research into new UK crops
content.standfirst: Researchers are testing crops such as lupins, chickpeas and lablab as heat and drought put pressure on familiar harvests. Their promise is still being assessed, and future yields will depend on where varieties can grow and withstand local conditions.

image.caption: A lupin bhaji, made with a crop researchers are testing for future UK growing.

sources.originalTitle: The protein-packed superfoods of the future – that you could grow in your garden

segments.body: This summer’s heat and drought damaged yields of several British crops, prompting researchers to investigate alternatives suited to hotter, drier conditions. At Southampton University, a government-funded network is working with farmers, food businesses and chefs to test crops including lupins and chickpeas.

segments.title: Testing new possibilities
segments.body: Lupins can be processed into flour and are drought tolerant, while chickpeas are already being grown by some UK farmers. Researchers say more work is needed to identify suitable varieties and locations, and to assess risks from pests and disease before farmers plant them at scale.

Changing conditions could also shift where familiar crops thrive: some fruit may become easier to grow further north, while warmer southern areas could suit crops such as melons and apricots. Researchers caution that late spring frosts and other local conditions could still damage crops, so the winners and losers are not yet certain.

content.headline: Northern lights have been visible across the UK, with more sightings possible
content.shortHeadline: Aurora sightings reach southern England
content.standfirst: The aurora borealis was seen as far south as Devon, Hampshire and Kent over the weekend. The Met Office says further sightings may be possible in clear skies until Tuesday, though visibility depends on conditions.

image.caption: Aurora over Sheerness, Kent, during recent UK sightings.

sources.originalTitle: Skies across the UK illuminated by the northern lights

segments.body: The northern lights illuminated skies across the UK on Friday and Saturday, with reports as far south as Devon, Hampshire and Kent. The Met Office said sightings could remain possible until Tuesday in Scotland and at similar geomagnetic longitudes if skies are clear.

segments.title: What causes the display
segments.body: Auroras form when charged particles associated with the solar wind interact with Earth’s magnetic field and collide with gases high in the atmosphere. Those collisions release light; oxygen and nitrogen produce different colours.

content.headline: Viral chart did not show Russian disinformation bots falling after data-centre
content.shortHeadline: Viral chart misread as evidence Russian troll bots had fallen
content.standfirst: A chart circulating after strikes on Russian data centres appears to track Yandex web crawlers, not social-media troll activity. The data source for a separate image purporting to show political bot activity is also unverified.

sources.originalTitle: The Yandex outage probably didn’t blitz Russian bots

segments.body: Online posts claimed Russian bot activity had plunged after Ukrainian drone strikes took data centres offline. But the widely shared chart citing Cloudflare data appears to measure automated Yandex web crawlers, which can index websites and support services, rather than social-media accounts spreading disinformation.

segments.title: Unverified figures
segments.body: A separate chart shared as evidence of a drop in activity around Germany’s AfD party has no established data source, and the original image did not identify the party. A computer scientist questioned its timeline, including a point dated in the future. Cloudflare data cited in the reporting indicates Russian bot traffic overall remained largely unchanged.

The reporting says many Yandex-operated services remained offline after the strikes, including its payments service. That disruption does not substantiate claims about disinformation networks; the article highlights how charts with unclear definitions and provenance can be misread and recirculated.

content.headline: US Air Force contract could give weather-balloon startup up to $49m
